interactions.summary: A student says Mucius should strike without certainty just to prove the will is real, and Jiang completes the story by showing Mucius miss, refuse to confess, and burn his own hand rather than let coercion master him.

A student reads Beatrice's distinction between absolute and contingent will after the Alcmaeon example, and Jiang glosses it as the kind of moral dilemma where two obligations collide and fear mixes force with consent.
interactions.speaker_attribution: reader quoting Beatrice with Jiang gloss

interactions.summary: Jiang marks the absolute-versus-contingent distinction as the next major concept the room has to unpack.

claims.claim: The student answering Jiang's Mucius prompt says decisive action matters more than certainty: killing either target would still prove the will was present.
Jiang presents Mucius as the man who acts under uncertainty, kills the wrong person, then proves his courage by refusing confession even under threat of being burned alive.
Beatrice's argument is that moral life often places people in situations where one wrong seems to answer another, as when filial obedience and murder collide in the Alcmaeon example.
The passage distinguishes an absolute will that never agrees to evil from a contingent will that consents out of fear when resistance seems likely to produce greater harm.
Jiang frames the absolute-versus-contingent split as a central key for reconciling Piccarda's innocence language with Beatrice's insistence that yielding still implicates the will.

signature_moments.moment: A student compresses courage into one brutal formula: strike anyway, because the act itself proves the will is alive.
signature_moments.source_phrase: I just kill, because I kill and it means my will is there
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns Jiang's Mucius story into a direct test of whether will means certainty or committed action under risk.

signature_moments.moment: Mucius answers torture by putting his own hand in the fire and effectively treating pain as irrelevant to the mission.
signature_moments.source_phrase: he just put his hand in the fire
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's most vivid image of an unbroken will surviving bodily threat.

signature_moments.moment: Beatrice solves the coercion puzzle by splitting the self into an absolute will that stays clean and a contingent will that caves from fear.
signature_moments.source_phrase: absolute will does not concur in wrong but the contingent will through fear
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the conceptual hinge for the rest of Jiang's Paradise discussion about responsibility under force.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: A classical example Jiang uses through Beatrice: a son ordered by his father to kill his mother, showing how moral duties can collide.
The fear-governed will that reacts to circumstances and can yield to force even when the deeper absolute will remains pointed toward the good.

chronology_notes.note: The packet moves from Mucius as a concrete image of fearless resolve into Beatrice's abstract distinction between absolute and contingent will, making the story function as an embodied preface to the doctrine.

uncertainty_notes.note: The ASR is noisy in Jiang's retelling of the king's dialogue with Mucius, but the core action is clear: Mucius refuses confession and burns his hand to demonstrate fearless resolve.
